newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Peru sign pacts to boost economic ties.
newsitem.headline: India, Peru sign pacts to boost economic ties.

text.p: Peru and India signed agreements to boost economic cooperation on Monday as President Alberto Fujimori began the official leg of a four-day visit to raise his nation's profile in India.
The Peruvian leader offered his country's vast mineral resources to Indian businessmen and in turn sought technology from the firms of fast-industrialising India.
Fujimori, who arrived on Sunday for his first visit to India, shared with Indian leaders views on common security issues linked to insurgency.
Peruvian troops killed 14 leftist guerrillas to end a 127-day hostage crisis in Lima last month.

"I think the most important aspect is trade ties," said Fujimori, who was set to address business leaders in New Delhi on Tuesday. "India has technology and at the same time, Peru has mineral resources that may be useful to India."
He spoke at the presidential palace, where he was received at a ceremonial welcome by President Shankar Dayal Sharma and Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.

Fujimori, who won power in 1990, has led a restructuring programme that aims to boost economic growth to 5.0 percent in 1997 from 2.8 percent last year. India began an economic reforms programme six years ago.

"Over the last few years, a dramatic economic transformation has taken place in Peru. This is a tribute to your leadership and the policies of your administration," President Sharma said at a banquet to honour Fujimori.

Peru and India signed six agreements, including one on promoting joint ventures and travel between the two countries to boost tourism and another on joint efforts to strengthen knowledge and expertise on Antarctica.
The other agreements were on consultations between the foreign offices, cooperation on diplomatic expertise, technical cooperation and agricultural research.

After the agreements were signed, Gujral said he hoped to visit Peru in the near future after an invitation from Fujimori. The two leaders said they had discussed "South-South" cooperation between developing countries during their talks.

"I think the world needs to keep peace in order to achieve development," Fujimori said at the presidential palace, speaking of a need to contain armed militancy, which is common to both Peru and India.
India is grappling with armed separatist movements in Kashmir, its northeast and pockets of the east and south.
Peruvian troops killed 14 rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement on April 22 while releasing 72 hostages who were being held in the Japanese ambassador's residence.
Last week, Peruvian security forces captured two military leaders of the Maoist Shining Path guerrilla group, which is feared to be starting a new campaign of violence.
"We share your view and are firmly convinced that no democratic government can make any concession whatsoever to the demands of terrorists..." Sharma said.
In 1996, India exported goods worth $41 million to Peru, mainly motorcycles, bicycles, tyres and tubes, three-wheel vehicles, pharmaceuticals and automobile and bicycle parts.
India's imports, mainly fishmeal, zinc and pima cotton, totalled $15 million.

Fujimori said at a news conference that Peru would support India's bid to win a permanent seat in a proposed expansion of the United Nations Security Council, which currently has 15 members, five of them permanent.
"India is the biggest democracy. We would support it, of course," Fujimori said.
